name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
title: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
answer: This page covers the use of AI systems to produce and test competing interpretations of statutes in litigation and regulatory disputes. It includes techniques for identifying textual ambiguity, mapping legislative history, and generating plausible readings that favor one side or the other. The focus is on how lawyers and legal researchers can use language models and retrieval tools to build arguments about what a statute means, rather than on predicting how a court will rule.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the use of AI systems to produce and test competing interpretations of statutes in litigation and regulatory disputes. It includes techniques for identifying textual ambiguity, mapping legislative history, and generating plausible readings that favor one side or the other. The focus is on how lawyers and legal researchers can use language models and retrieval tools to build arguments about what a statute means, rather than on predicting how a court will rule.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on general purpose large language models connected to legal document collections through retrieval augmented generation. Statutes, regulations, committee reports, and prior court decisions are indexed in vector databases so the model can pull relevant passages before drafting an interpretation. Some teams fine tune smaller models on annotated examples of statutory construction canons, but most use prompt based workflows with commercial or open weight models.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A lawyer typically starts by stating the statutory provision and the interpretive question. The system then retrieves related text and precedent, and produces several candidate readings, each with supporting and opposing citations. The lawyer reviews these outputs, edits them, and uses them to stress test the opposing side's likely arguments. The method is iterative: each round of generated text is checked against the actual statutory language and the jurisdiction's rules of construction.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are fabricated case citations, leakage of confidential case strategy into third party models, and over reliance on a model's confident but wrong reading. Lawyers must verify every cited source and keep client specific material out of unapproved systems. Provenance matters: any generated interpretation should be traceable to the exact statutory text, legislative history, or precedent that supports it. The site's 210 compliance and regulation pages track the professional responsibility rules that apply to AI assisted legal research.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The next few years will likely bring legal specific models that are better at following canons of construction and less prone to inventing authority. Tools will move from drafting single interpretations to running structured adversarial simulations, where one model argues for a reading and another attacks it. Integration with state bill tracking, including the 6,825 state AI bills currently monitored on this site, may let lawyers test how a proposed statute would be interpreted under different judicial philosophies.
